responsive-website-tester.quickAnswer: Enter any website URL and see how it looks at popular device widths: 390px phones, 768px tablets, 1024px laptops, and 1440px desktops. Use the presets or drag the slider for any custom width, and the page reloads live inside a resizable frame so you can spot layout breaks quickly.
keyFacts: Responsive design means one site adapts its layout to any screen width.
The most common breakpoints cluster around 390px (phones), 768px (tablets), and 1024px+ (desktops).
This tool renders the real page in an iframe at the width you choose.
Horizontal scrolling at phone widths is the most common responsive bug.
Touch targets should be at least 44px so buttons are tappable on phones.
howTo: Enter the full website URL starting with https://.
Pick a device preset or set a custom width with the slider.
Inspect the rendered page inside the frame.
Try several widths to catch layout breaks.
Fix issues in your CSS, then re-test the same URL.
responsive-website-tester.formula:

responsive-website-tester.workedExample:
Testing https://jaurtools.com at 390px shows the mobile layout: navigation collapses, tool cards stack vertically, and text stays readable without zooming.
At 1440px the same page shows the full desktop grid.
If a table overflows at 390px, that is a responsive bug to fix with stacked cards or smaller padding.
benefits: Spot layout breaks at real device widths in seconds.
No device lab needed: test from any computer.
Custom widths cover foldables and ultrawide screens.
Live reload of the real page, not a screenshot.
limitations: Some sites block iframe embedding (X-Frame-Options) and show a blank frame.
The frame simulates width only, not touch input or device performance.
Login-walled pages cannot be tested without a session.
Very heavy pages may load slowly inside the frame.

faqs.q: Why is the frame blank for some sites?
faqs.a: Those sites send X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors headers that forbid embedding. It is a security choice by the site owner, not a tool bug.

faqs.q: Does this replace testing on a real phone?
faqs.a: No. It catches most layout issues fast, but real devices also reveal touch, performance, and font-rendering differences. Test on a phone before launch.
Only if this page can reach your machine. Public URLs work best; localhost generally does not load from a hosted page.

faqs.q: What width should I design for first?
faqs.a: Start at 360-390px (common phones), then scale up. Mobile-first CSS with min-width breakpoints is the standard approach.

faqs.q: Is the tested URL sent anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The URL stays in your browser; the iframe loads the site directly from your device like a normal visit.

responsive-website-tester.assumptionNote: Width simulation only: the frame cannot emulate touch input, device performance, or OS font rendering. Some sites block embedding.
